sources.title: The transnational historiography of a dynastic transition, Modern Asian Studies
sources.note: Peer-reviewed framing of 1618 to 1683 as a plural struggle among Ming, Qing and other claimants rather than one handover.

sources.title: Lynn A. Struve, The Southern Ming, 1644-1662, Cambridge History of China
sources.note: Authoritative political and social history of the Southern Ming courts, commanders, refugees, unrest and final defeat.

sources.title: David Faure, The End of Empire, Emperor and Ancestor
sources.note: Scholarly account of competing 1646 Guangdong courts, Zhaoqing, Guangzhou and Pearl River resistance.

sources.title: Lynn A. Struve, The Ming-Qing Conflict: A Historiography and Source Guide
sources.note: Indiana University source guide assessing records for Sun Kewang, Anlong, Li Dingguo and the move to Kunming.

sources.title: Epistolary Activities in the Early Southern Ming Period, Journal of the European Association for Chinese Studies
sources.note: Peer-reviewed study of wartime letters, disrupted transmission and Sun Kewang control of the Yongli court at Anlong.

sources.title: The Qing Empire and Its Military, Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Military History
sources.note: Scholarly synthesis of Qing conquest armies, autonomous feudatories, the 1673 revolt and its defeat in 1681.

sources.title: Jonathan D. Spence, The Kang-hsi Reign, Cambridge History of China
sources.note: Authoritative account of Kangxi rule and consolidation, with a dedicated map of suppressing the Three Feudatories.

sources.title: Qing Military Institutions and Their Effects on Government, Economy, and Society
sources.note: Peer-reviewed analysis of campaign finance, Banner and Green Standard forces, supply burdens and post-1681 security.

sources.title: Kenneth M. Swope, On the Trail of the Yellow Tiger, University of Nebraska Press
sources.note: Academic monograph on war, trauma, rival armies, social dislocation and reconstruction in southwest China during the Ming-Qing transition.

sources.title: The Shogun’s Chinese Partners, Journal of Asian Studies
sources.note: Peer-reviewed study distinguishing the maritime Zheng organization and its Japanese relations from inland southwest regimes.

sources.title: Xing Hang, Conflict and Commerce in Maritime East Asia, Cambridge University Press excerpt
sources.note: Cambridge book introduction tracing the Zheng organization, its Three Feudatories alliance, 1681 reversal and 1683 surrender.

sources.title: Yongli tongbao coin, British Museum 1886,1006.780
sources.note: Museum record for a four-character Yongli copper-alloy cash coin issued by Zhu Youlang and dated 1646 to 1659.

sources.title: Zheng Chenggong Yongli tongbao coin, British Museum 1883,0802.1480
sources.note: Museum record for a Yongli-inscribed cash coin minted in Japan and issued by Zheng Chenggong from 1651 to 1670.

sources.title: The Art of Dissent in 17th-Century China, Metropolitan Museum of Art
sources.note: Museum synthesis of Ming loyalist painting, calligraphy, trauma, refusal of Qing service and new individual styles.

sources.title: A Tale of Dynastic Change in China, Archivum Historicum Societatis Iesu
sources.note: Peer-reviewed correction of Jesuit accounts about baptized members of the Yongli household and their European representation.

sources.title: De-centering Chinese History, Journal of Chinese History
sources.note: Peer-reviewed account of tusi reciprocity and limited Han cultural reach in seventeenth-century Yunnan and Guizhou.

sources.title: Lady Qu’s Inscriptions: Literacy and Sovereignty in a Native Domain, Journal of Asian Studies
sources.note: Peer-reviewed study of Chinese and Nasu inscriptions, Yi sovereignty, female rule and strategic multilingual self-presentation.

sources.title: The Cant of Conquest: Tusi Offices and China’s Southwest Frontier
sources.note: Scholarly analysis of sixteenth- and seventeenth-century Guizhou texts and the shift between indirect and direct rule.

sources.title: Tributary Labour Relations in China During the Ming-Qing Transition
sources.note: Peer-reviewed study of bond service, conquest violence, work relations and elite-focused accommodation during the transition.

sources.title: Women, Families, and Gender Relations, Cambridge History of China
sources.note: Scholarly synthesis of seventeenth-century commoner households, gendered labor, lineages, mobility and women’s medicine.

sources.title: Early Modern Patterns, 1500-1740, Chinese Diasporas
sources.note: Scholarly account of split families, male migration, female domestic labor, lineage strategies and frontier intermarriage.

sources.title: Work Ethics and Work Valuations in Ming China, International Review of Social History
sources.note: Peer-reviewed evidence on rural subsistence, market towns, agricultural tasks, textile work and gendered labor.

sources.title: Ming model feast dishes, British Museum 1927,1214.9
sources.note: Museum discussion of rice in southern China, varied foods, feasting and the limits of elite burial models.

sources.title: Nine Sloughs: Climate History of the Yuan and Ming Dynasties
sources.note: Peer-reviewed reconstruction of late Ming weather, harvest shocks, famine and extreme grain-price evidence.

sources.title: Social and economic factors in Jingdezhen porcelain, 1620-1683
sources.note: Peer-reviewed study of porcelain production through dynastic breakdown, rebellion, markets and changing patronage.

sources.title: Printing and Book Culture in Late Imperial China
sources.note: Scholarly collection on urban and rural publishers, expanding audiences, niche markets, non-Han texts and genealogy printing.

sources.title: Education in Premodern China and Japan, Oxford Handbook of the History of Education
sources.note: Scholarly overview of curricula, schools, examinations, teachers, literacy and unequal educational access by gender.

sources.title: Community Schools and the State in Ming China, American Historical Review
sources.note: Academic review explaining community schools, basic literacy, Confucian ethics, local patrons and the gap between mandate and access.

sources.title: Children playing in the palace garden, Metropolitan Museum of Art
sources.note: Museum record for an elite Ming image of twenty-two boys, hobbyhorses, games and a masonry slide.

sources.title: Birthday Portraits of an Official and His Wife, Metropolitan Museum Journal
sources.note: Museum research on late Ming household portraiture, rank badges, wedding dress and women’s use of status-marked clothing.

sources.title: Freeing Chinese Men on the María Luz, Journal of Global History
sources.note: Peer-reviewed discussion of the Qing queue as compulsory male subjecthood and a repeatedly contested political sign.

sources.title: Chinese Materia medica, seventeenth century, Wellcome Collection
sources.note: Collection record for the 1638 illustrated edition cataloguing 452 medicinal substances, features, seasons and recipes.

sources.title: Seventeenth-century Chinese acupuncture chart, Wellcome Collection
sources.note: Collection record for a Ming Tianqi-period woodblock diagram of acu-moxa points and named channels.

sources.title: Response to Epidemic Disease in Ancient China and its Characteristics
sources.note: Peer-reviewed review of prescriptions, drug shops, isolation, corpse burial, ritual, variolation and late Ming epidemic theory.

sources.title: Nightsoil and the Great Divergence, Journal of Global History
sources.note: Peer-reviewed global history of urban waste collection, fertilizer markets and sanitation from 1500 to 1900.

sources.title: Writing Yunnan into China, International Journal of Asian Studies
sources.note: Peer-reviewed evidence for Yunnan granaries, irrigation, walls, bridges and the political language attached to public works.

sources.title: Huangguoshu Scenic Area and Tunpu settlements, UNESCO World Heritage Centre
sources.note: UNESCO description of Guizhou Ming-Qing courtyard houses, stone construction, military-settler villages and irrigation works.

sources.title: Lingqu Canal, UNESCO World Heritage Centre
sources.note: UNESCO technical description of the enduring canal, locks, weirs, transport, irrigation and Pearl-Yangtze watershed connection.

proposedOverrides.summary: An atlas umbrella for successive Southern Ming and rebel-held southwest zones, preserved from 1650 to 1715 despite historical endings in 1662 and 1681.

batchIdentityNotes: The exact imported id post-ming-warlords is preserved, but the card treats it as an atlas umbrella rather than one historical state name.
The exact approximate interval is 1650 to 1715 in two observed border files. It spans successive and opposed regimes rather than a continuous government.
No appliesTo alias is added. Ming Dynasty, Qing Dynasty, Zheng maritime history, Taiwan and neighboring records remain distinct.
The target geometry is an unchanged 166-position MultiPolygon in 1650 and 1700 with SHA-256 b32847b1355f4dc47a2d9ed2b13eb16ecce5ee3ce139ae2cf76086498e2085d1.
The 1700 persistence is historically impossible for both the Yongli court and Three Feudatories revolt, so the card exposes rather than naturalizes it.
The 1715 disappearance is an atlas redraw into Qing geometry, not a historical fall. The override records fell null and no successor or predecessor arrays are inferred.
The writing sample is the target-period Yongli cash legend 永曆通寶 with pinyin, translation, reading order and non-facsimile caveat.
Daily-life evidence separates general late imperial comparisons, material objects and nearby surviving infrastructure from secure exact southwest evidence.
